As his inspection tour carries him deeper into the outer colonies, each dojo reveals further impossible divergences—strikes that land before intention, blocks against attacks occurring in other zip codes—and he stumbles into an ancient schism between two schools: the Honorbound, who insist reality's degrading rules must be obeyed *precisely because* they are degrading, and the Formless, who teach students to exploit every glitch as a combat technique, arguing that a universe this shoddily maintained deserves no philosophical loyalty. Semyon, a man whose entire identity rests on enforcing standardized forms in a cosmos that no longer has a standard, resolves to travel to the legendary First Dojo at the network's edge to file his complaint with whatever authority built this reality—only to discover the bureaucratic chain of command extends upward through nested simulations, each with its own fluorescent-lit certification bureau and its own Semyon, and there is no home office left to return to, just an infinite regression of lobbies where the forms keep quietly, grotesquely changing.

# Seven Structural Beats for the Semyon Krakauer Story
## Adapted from the Architecture of *Cathedral*

---

## Beat 1: The Audit Record and the Voice That Doesn't Know Itself

**What Must Happen:** Before any anomaly appears, before the plot moves, Semyon must establish himself through retrospective narration — his job, his routes, his eleven thousand documented repetitions of the Crane Sequence's 47th movement. He must tell us about the Pan-Galactic Martial Arts Certification Bureau, the strip-mall dojos, the fluorescent-lit stations, the forms he carries in triplicate. He must convey that he is a man who has built his entire identity around recognizing deviation — and that he has never once asked what the forms are *for*.

**The Technique to Employ:** *First-person retrospective narration as indirect self-portraiture.* Every detail Semyon chooses to share about the Bureau, about the dojos, about the indifferent practitioners who endure his inspections, must reveal something he doesn't know about himself. He should fixate on petty grievances — the station coffee, colleagues who don't return his messages, students who smirk during compliance reviews — the way Carver's narrator fixates on Beulah's name. The reader must understand, before Semyon does, that he is describing a life of total spiritual vacancy. His precision about kata angles is the precision of a man who has nothing else. His contempt for the outer colonies is the contempt of someone who understands, at some frequency below consciousness, that the center he serves may not exist.

**Why This Must Come First:** The reader's relationship to Semyon — simultaneous dependence on his voice and superiority to his understanding — is the engine of the whole narrative. If we don't split from him early, if we don't see more than he sees in his own words, nothing that follows will carry its proper weight. The comedy of his pettiness is the setup for the eventual horror of his condition. He must be repellent and compulsively readable for the same reason Carver's narrator is: his honesty about his own smallness is so total that it becomes a strange, unwitting vulnerability. He doesn't hide his worst instincts. He catalogs them on official forms. He just doesn't recognize the form he's filling out is a confession.

**The Trap to Avoid:** Do not let the worldbuilding upstage the voice. The Pan-Galactic Bureau, the stations, the dojos — all of it must come through Semyon's bureaucratic diction, not through expository architecture. The universe should feel fluorescent and banal and slightly wrong, not spectacular. If the world feels like science fiction, the story fails. It must feel like a workplace.

---

## Beat 2: The Elbow Bends Wrong

**What Must Happen:** During a routine inspection at an unremarkable dojo on an unremarkable station, Semyon observes the 47th movement of the Crane Sequence. A practitioner's elbow bends in a direction elbows have never bent. Not grotesquely — not a horror-movie contortion. Just *wrong.* A few degrees past the limit of what anatomy permits. Semyon marks it on his form. He asks the instructor about it. The instructor looks at him blankly. The students repeat the movement. It bends the same way. Semyon demonstrates the correct form. His own elbow doesn't bend quite the direction he remembers either — or does it? He isn't sure. No one else finds this remarkable.

**The Technique to Employ:** *Defamiliarization through the expectation gap — the auditor's frame of reference fails.* Exactly as Carver has his narrator describe Robert through a series of negations (no dark glasses, no cane), Semyon must describe the anomaly through what it is *not.* The elbow does not bend correctly. The practitioners do not react. The instructor does not understand the question. Semyon's entire perceptual apparatus — eleven thousand documented repetitions — should make him the most qualified observer in the universe, and yet his expertise is precisely what makes the wrongness unbearable. He is the only one who can see the deviation because he is the only one who ever cared about the standard. The sighted man among the blind. But the inversion must be planted here too: maybe the others aren't failing to see. Maybe Semyon is the one still clinging to a measurement that no longer measures anything.

**Why This Must Be Played Small:** The temptation will be to make the wrong elbow spectacular. Resist this absolutely. The wrongness must be almost administrative — a discrepancy in a form, a box that can't be checked. The horror is not body horror. The horror is *procedural.* Something doesn't comply, and there is no one to report it to who cares. The cosmic dread must enter through a clipboard. This is the story's equivalent of Robert walking through the door without dark glasses: the narrator's pop-cultural frame dissolves on contact with the actual thing.

---

## Beat 3: The Inspection Deepens — Cataloging the Impossible

**What Must Happen:** Semyon continues his audit route into the outer colonies. Each dojo reveals further divergences, and he documents them all with escalating forensic precision. Strikes that land before intention. Blocks against attacks occurring in other zip codes. A kata where the practitioner's foot is on the ground and not on the ground simultaneously, and the scorecard simply says "adequate." Semyon fills out deviation reports. He cross-references historical footage. He calls the Bureau. No one answers, or they answer and don't understand the question, or they understand the question and tell him the forms have been updated and he must not have received the memo.

**The Technique to Employ:** *Close behavioral observation as a substitute for emotional engagement — the anthropologist noting impossible phenomena with bureaucratic calm.* This is the Carver dinner-scene technique: Semyon watches the impossible the way the narrator watches Robert eat. He catalogs mechanics because he cannot engage with meaning. He can describe the exact angle of a strike that violates causality but cannot articulate *why this should concern anyone.* The accumulation of details should be generous and almost comic — a lavish abundance of wrongness — contrasting sharply with Semyon's emotional scarcity. The dojos themselves should feel full, alive, practiced-in; the students thrive in their impossible forms. The poverty is entirely Semyon's. He is a man with a ruler in a world that has moved past Euclidean geometry, and he keeps measuring.

**What Must Quietly Happen Underneath:** Each dojo should feel slightly more lived-in, more communal, more purposeful than the last — even as the divergences grow more extreme. The students are *better* martial artists than they should be. The impossible techniques *work.* This is the equivalent of Robert out-inhabiting the narrator's own home: the "deviant" practitioners possess a fluency in their reality that Semyon, the supposed authority, entirely lacks. He should register this half-consciously at best — noticing that students seem happy, that instructors seem calm, that the dojos hum with something he doesn't have a form for.

---

## Beat 4: The Schism — The Mediating Framework Falls Asleep

**What Must Happen:** Semyon discovers — through an instructor who finally takes his confusion seriously, or through a document found in a dojo's back office, or through a late-night conversation at a station bar — the existence of the two schools: the Honorbound and the Formless. The Honorbound insist that reality's degrading rules must be obeyed *precisely because* they are degrading — fidelity to the standard is a moral act even when the standard is collapsing. The Formless teach students to exploit every glitch as a combat technique, arguing that a universe this shoddily maintained deserves no philosophical loyalty. The schism is ancient. Everyone in the outer colonies knows about it. Semyon, the Bureau's representative, has never heard of either school. The framework he has served his whole career — the notion that there is one correct form and his job is to enforce it — goes to sleep.

**The Technique to Employ:** *Removal of the mediating structure to force confrontation.* In *Cathedral,* the wife falls asleep, stripping away the social lubricant between narrator and Robert. Here, what "falls asleep" is the Bureau itself — not literally, but as a operative belief system. Semyon's credential, his clipboard, his entire professional identity, is revealed to be not wrong but *irrelevant.* He has been adjudicating a debate that has been raging for generations, and no one told him because no one considered the Bureau a participant. The effect must be the same as the wife going unconscious on the sofa: the comfortable structure that let Semyon navigate without genuine encounter is suddenly removed, and he must face the anomalies — face *reality* — without his forms to hide behind.

**The Critical Emotional Note:** Semyon must not simply learn about the schism as exposition. It must *cost* him something. The Honorbound position should be uncomfortably close to his own — they believe in standards — but their reasoning reveals that they know the standards are arbitrary, that they practice obedience as a *philosophical choice* in the face of cosmic decay, not because the forms are true. This is devastating to Semyon. He has never *chosen* his obedience. He has simply assumed the forms were correct. The Honorbound are monks; Semyon is a meter maid. The distinction should humiliate him the way Robert's easy competence humiliates Carver's narrator. Meanwhile, the Formless position should be terrifying but exhilarating — a philosophy of joyful exploitation of the broken. They are alive in a way Semyon is not. Their dojo should be the most vibrant place he has ever stood in.

**Structural Function:** This beat must be the pivot. Everything before it is Semyon's world. Everything after it is the world he didn't know he inhabited. The drawbridge lowers.

---

## Beat 5: The Attempt to Describe the Correct Form — And the Failure

**What Must Happen:** Semyon tries to articulate — to himself, to someone, perhaps to a Formless instructor who genuinely and non-mockingly asks — what the *correct* 47th movement of the Crane Sequence looks like. He tries to demonstrate it. He tries to explain what a regulation-compliant kata *is.* And he cannot. Not because he's forgotten, but because the attempt to describe correctness reveals that he has never understood it. He knows the angle of the elbow. He knows the degree of rotation. But when pressed on *what makes this the right form* — why this angle and not another, what the Crane Sequence expresses, what it was built to do — he has nothing. He has been enforcing a standard for his entire career and he cannot tell you what the standard *means.* He says something equivalent to "I just can't do it."

**The Technique to Employ:** *Dramatized failure of articulation as revelation of deeper emptiness — the inability to describe the correct form as the discovery that one never possessed it.* This is the cathedral scene. The blind man asks, "What does a cathedral look like?" Here, the question is: "What does the correct form look like — *really*?" And Semyon discovers, in real time, that his expertise was always mechanical. He can cite compliance codes. He can measure angles. But the kata was designed to express something — some principle of movement, combat philosophy, relationship between body and universe — and he has documented it eleven thousand times without ever once asking what it expressed. The question is Socratic. Semyon's ignorance is revealed to him through the act of trying to teach.

**Why This Must Be the Emotional Nadir:** This is Semyon's "I just can't do it" — his first moment of genuine humility. It should not be played for comedy, even though everything around it may be absurd. The humor drops away. A man who defined himself as the keeper of correct form realizes he doesn't know what correct form is. His confession should feel like the narrator's in *Cathedral:* not eloquent, not self-pitying, just a man running out of words, standing at the edge of his own vocabulary, looking into the gap. This moment earns everything that follows. Without it, the finale is spectacle. With it, the finale is grace.

---

## Beat 6: The Journey to the First Dojo — Drawing the Form Together

**What Must Happen:** Semyon resolves to travel to the legendary First Dojo at the network's edge to file his complaint — his deviation report — with whatever authority built this reality. The journey itself should feel like a collaborative act, not a solo quest. Someone accompanies him, or guides him, or the journey requires him to move through increasingly impossible spaces where the old forms and the new ones blur. He must *do something with his body.* Perhaps he must perform kata to pass through checkpoints or translate between dojos. Perhaps a Formless practitioner places their hands over his hands and shows him how the impossible movements work — and for the first time, his body does something his clipboard never allowed. The key: the transformation is kinesthetic, not intellectual. He doesn't *learn* the truth. He *moves* through it. He draws the cathedral.

**The Technique to Employ:** *Collaborative physical action as the vehicle for transformation — showing change through the body rather than the mind.* Exactly as Carver refuses to give his narrator an intellectual revelation and instead puts a pen in his hand with Robert's hand on top, this story must make Semyon *move.* His body must do something new. The prose style should remain Semyon's — the same flat, bureaucratic, fussy diction — but now the simplicity should feel generative rather than reductive. His step-by-step description of performing an impossible kata should build the way the narrator's accumulating lines build a cathedral. Sentence by sentence, the form assembles. The instrument of transcendence should be as mundane as Carver's pen and paper bag: a regulation practice mat, a standard-issue gi, a compliance checklist turned over and used as scratch paper. The sublime located in the utterly bureaucratic.

**The Power Inversion:** Just as the blind man guides the sighted man in *Cathedral,* someone Semyon has previously condescended to — a student, an outer-colony instructor, a Formless practitioner — must become his guide. The auditor is audited. The one who measured is measured. But it must not be punitive. It must be generous. The guide must be patient and kind in the way Robert is patient and kind: not because Semyon deserves it, but because that's simply who they are.

---

## Beat 7: The Infinite Regression of Lobbies — "I Didn't Feel Like I Was Inside Anything"

**What Must Happen:** Semyon reaches the First Dojo and discovers it is a certification bureau. It has its own fluorescent lighting, its own deviation forms, its own Semyon — another auditor, perhaps slightly different, perhaps worryingly identical — who is filing a complaint about anomalies in *his* reality. The bureaucratic chain of command extends upward through nested simulations. Each level has its own Bureau. Each Bureau has its own version of the forms. And the forms keep changing. There is no home office. There
narrative_story:
# The Deviation Report

## I.

I want to say right off that I had nothing against the outer colonies. I want to make that clear. Some auditors—Petrov, for instance, or Danziger before she transferred to Aquatic Forms—would openly gripe about the assignments, the station food, the recycled air that always tasted like someone else's Tuesday. Not me. I had my preferences, sure. Everyone has preferences. But I kept them off the forms. The forms were sacred. That was the whole point.

My name is Semyon Krakauer and for fourteen years I served as a Level 3 Compliance Auditor for the Pan-Galactic Martial Arts Certification Bureau, which people either called the Bureau or called nothing because most people had never heard of it. My territory was the Cygnus-Vela corridor, stations 4100 through 4700, with occasional overflows into the Kepler margin when Petrov called in sick, which was often. Petrov had problems with his back. He had problems with lots of things. But the back was the one he put on the forms.

The job was this: I traveled to registered dojos, observed practitioners performing standardized kata sequences, and evaluated their compliance with Bureau Form 77-K, the Universal Movement Certification Rubric. Forty-seven movements in the Crane Sequence. Thirty-one in the Plow. Twenty-two in the Bridge, which people always underestimated because of the count, but which had more micro-transitions per movement than any other sanctioned form. I had documented eleven thousand, three hundred and nine performances of the Crane Sequence's 47th movement alone. That's the terminal strike—the one where the left arm extends at full rotation while the right foot completes its inward arc to rest position. The elbow must reach, upon full extension, an angle of one hundred seventy-four degrees relative to the upper arm. Not one-eighty. People assumed one-eighty. One-eighty is a locked joint. One-seventy-four permits the micro-flexion that distinguishes a living strike from a mechanical one. I had measured this. I had documented this. Eleven thousand, three hundred and nine times.

Nobody asked me to memorize the number. But I kept a log. I kept a log of my logs. This was not Bureau policy. This was initiative.

The dojos themselves were what you'd expect. Strip-mall spaces on the commercial levels of mid-range stations, sandwiched between hydroponic grocery outlets and the places that filled your atmospheric scrubbers for you. Some had windows looking out at the docking arrays. Most didn't. Fluorescent lighting, ninety percent of them. The Bureau's Facilities Compliance division—separate from my division, though we shared a floor on Station 4412 before they moved us—had issued a recommendation in the 4060s about full-spectrum lighting for practice spaces, something about circadian alignment, but it was a recommendation, not a mandate, and nobody followed recommendations. I barely followed mandates.

The practitioners were another thing I had opinions about but kept off the forms. Most of them were hobbyists. Station workers looking for exercise, or something to do between shifts that wasn't drinking or staring at a wall. They signed up for eight-week sessions, bought gis that still had the fold marks in them, and performed the movements with the enthusiasm of people renewing a parking permit. Which was fine. The Bureau didn't require enthusiasm. The Bureau required compliance. Angle of the elbow. Arc of the foot. Breath count on the transitions. There was a box for each on Form 77-K and I filled them in with the mechanical pencil I brought from home, not the Bureau-issued ones which smeared.

The instructors were marginally better, though the certification requirements for instructors in the outer colonies had been quietly lowered in the 4040s, a policy decision I had formally objected to in a memo that was acknowledged but not responded to. On Station 4400, which I visited with dependable regularity, there was an instructor named Yeong-Su who had once, during a compliance review, actually smirked at me. Not at anything I'd said. At the form itself. At Form 77-K. He'd glanced at it while I was marking the Crane Sequence evaluations for his intermediate class and he'd looked at the little boxes—the ones for elbow angle, wrist rotation, hip alignment—and the corner of his mouth had gone up, just slightly, the way you'd smile at a child who showed you a drawing of gravity.

I documented the smirk. Not on 77-K. On 77-K Supplemental, Section 14: Instructor Disposition and Professional Bearing. There was a box for that, too.

What I'm trying to say is that I was thorough. That was my function. I traveled the corridor, I observed the movements, I noted the deviations, and I filed the deviations with the Bureau's Central Compliance Office on Station 4001, which I had visited once and which was smaller than I'd expected. Beige walls. The coffee was bad. Yoon, the intake officer, had a plant on her desk that was either dying or a species I didn't recognize. She processed my reports without reading them. I know she didn't read them because I once, as an experiment, included a note on page four of a deviation filing that said, *If you are reading this, please contact me at extension 4412-90. I have a question about the Crane Sequence that I think is important.* She never called. Nobody ever called.

It didn't bother me. I want to be clear about that. I had my route, my forms, my schedule. The stations came and went through the shuttle windows like beads on a wire, one fluorescent box after another. I ate at the same cafeteria on each station. I slept in Bureau-rate lodgings, always interior rooms, always with the same hum of atmospheric processors that was just different enough from station to station that I could never quite get used to it. I could never quite sleep. I would lie there in the half-dark and think about the Crane Sequence, running through it in my head, each angle and arc, checking my mental model against the standard the way you'd check a watch against a clock that was itself set against some larger, more authoritative clock somewhere, the original clock, the one all the others were trying to be.

I never asked who set the original clock. That wasn't my department.

---

## II.

The elbow was on Station 4413. I remember the station because it was one stop past my home station and I almost never took assignments there—it felt like mowing your neighbor's lawn when your own was overgrown, which mine was, figuratively. But Petrov was out again, back problems, and the dojo on 4413 was overdue for its triennial review, and so on a Tuesday in the second quarter of the 4077th year I walked into the Keening Crane Dojo on Level 14, Commercial Block C, between a scrubber repair shop and a place that sold rice.

It was a nothing dojo. Twenty students, four classes a week, an instructor named Dahl whose certification I'd spot-checked three years prior and found adequate. The lighting was fluorescent, naturally. The mats were regulation gray with two small tears I made a note of. Seven students were present for the evaluation, which was above the minimum of five, so I didn't need to reschedule. They stood in two rows, barefoot, in gis of varying whiteness. One of the gis had a stain near the collar that might have been soy sauce. I made a note of this too.

They began the Crane Sequence. I sat on the folding chair Dahl had placed for me near the wall, Form 77-K on my clipboard, mechanical pencil in hand. The first forty-six movements were unremarkable. I checked boxes. Breath count on the opening transition was slightly rushed for the student in the back-left corner—a heavyset woman with short hair who seemed to be thinking about something else—but within tolerance. Hip alignment was acceptable across the group. Wrist rotation was sloppy but certifiable.

Movement 47.

The students extended their left arms. Their right feet completed the inward arc. And the elbow of the man in the front row—young, medium build, unremarkable in every dimension I had a box for—bent at approximately one hundred eighty-nine degrees.

I looked at my protractor. I looked at his arm. I looked at my protractor again.

One hundred eighty-nine degrees is not possible. An elbow does not bend past one hundred eighty degrees because one hundred eighty degrees is the structural limit of the hinge joint. At one-eighty, the arm is straight. At one-eighty-nine, the arm is—I didn't have a word for what the arm was. It was going the wrong direction. Just slightly. Just a few degrees past the place where the arm should stop and the arm had not stopped. It wasn't grotesque. That's what unnerved me. If his arm had twisted backward like something from a horror feed, I could have categorized it: injury, deformity, prank. But this was quiet. This was a few degrees. This was an arm that simply did not acknowledge the boundary I had been measuring against for fourteen years.

I put my pencil down. I picked it up. I wrote on the form: *47th movement. Left elbow. Exceeds anatomical range. Approximately 189°. Recommend follow-up.*

Then I looked at the other students. The heavyset woman in the back. The teenager beside her. The three in the second row. All of them had their arms extended. All of them were at approximately the same angle.

"Excuse me," I said.

Dahl looked over. He'd been adjusting a student's foot placement.

"The 47th movement," I said. "The terminal extension."

"Yes?"

"The elbow angle. In the standard, the left elbow reaches one hundred seventy-four degrees on full extension."

Dahl looked at me. Not blankly, exactly. More the way someone looks at you when you've said something in a language they used to speak but haven't thought about in years.

"Can you have them repeat the movement?" I said.

He could. He did. They repeated it. The elbows bent the same way. Past one-eighty. Past the place where elbows end. Just slightly past, like a sentence that goes on one word longer than grammar permits and somehow you understand it anyway but you know—you *know*—there was no room for that word.

"Could you demonstrate the correct form for me?" I said to Dahl.

He performed the 47th movement. His elbow did the same thing. One-eighty-nine, or close to it. He held the position and looked at me as if asking whether I'd gotten what I needed.

"That's not—" I said. "The elbow doesn't go there."

"Go where?"

"Past straight."

Dahl looked at his own arm. He flexed it slightly. The arm moved the way arms move if you've never thought too carefully about how arms move.

"Show me," he said. Not hostile. Just patient, the way instructors are patient with slow students.

I stood up from the folding chair. I placed the clipboard on the seat. I stood next to Dahl, in front of the two rows of students who watched me with polite, mild curiosity—the same curiosity they might have had for a plumber explaining why a pipe wasn't up to code.

I performed the 47th movement.

I extended my left arm. My right foot completed its inward arc. I focused on the elbow, on reaching precisely one hundred seventy-four degrees, on stopping at the exact point where the standard said stop.

My arm extended. And it felt—normal. It felt like it always had. One-seventy-four. I was almost certain.

But I couldn't see my own elbow. Not the way I could see theirs.  I turned my wrist slightly to get a better angle of view, and something in the rotation felt a degree off, or two degrees, and then I wasn't sure if the degree I was feeling was the deviation or if the deviation was the thing I was correcting *for*, and for a moment—just a moment—I did not know where my arm was in space.

"Looks fine to me," Dahl said.

I sat back down. I picked up the clipboard. In the box for the 47th movement, I had already written my note. I looked at it. Neat handwriting, mechanical pencil, no smears. *Exceeds anatomical range.* The words were precise. They were correct. They described a thing that I had seen. And no one in the room—not Dahl, not the seven students, not the heavyset woman who was now stretching her calves—found the thing I had described to be in any way remarkable.

I completed the form. I rated the dojo adequate. I walked back to the station's transit corridor and stood at the window for a while, watching a freighter move slowly across the docking array, and I thought about the fact that in fourteen years and eleven thousand documented performances of the 47th movement, I had never once seen an elbow do what those elbows had done, and the only possible conclusions were that every elbow before today had been correct and today's were wrong, or that today's elbows were always like this and I had never noticed, or that the elbows had changed.

None of these conclusions had a box on the form.

I filed the deviation report that evening. I attached my protractor readings. I sent it to Central Compliance on Station 4001, to Yoon's desk, to the place where deviation reports went to become part of the record that no one read.

Then I went to bed and did not sleep.

---

## III.

Over the next five weeks, I visited nineteen dojos across the outer run of my territory—Stations 4500 through 4688, the stretch of the corridor where it tapers toward the Kepler margin and the stations get smaller and further apart and the air starts to taste more honestly of recycled sweat. I was, technically, ahead of schedule. I had moved up six triennial reviews and requested three spot inspections that were within my discretionary authority but that I had never previously invoked. If anyone at the Bureau noticed the acceleration, they didn't mention it. No one at the Bureau mentioned much.

I will describe what I found. I will describe it the way I recorded it, which is to say precisely, because precision was the only tool I had and I was holding onto it the way a man in a current holds onto a rope that may or may not be tied to something.

Station 4501, the Falling Leaf Dojo. Crane Sequence, movement 12: the open-palm guard. The standard specifies that the right hand rises to temple height with fingers spread at fifteen-degree intervals. In this dojo, two of the six practitioners produced an open-palm guard where the space between the fingers was not measurable. Not because the fingers were closed—they were visibly apart—but because my protractor, when placed against the hand, returned no reading. The needle didn't move. I tried three times. The fingers were spread and the angle between them was not a number. The instructor, a quiet woman named Vasquez, asked if I needed water.

Station 4523, the Iron Root Dojo. Plow Sequence, movement 8: the descending block. The standard specifies that the forearm descends at forty-five degrees to intercept an incoming strike from above. In this dojo, the forearm of the lead student descended and intercepted a strike that was not occurring. There was no partner. There was no incoming attack. The student was performing solo kata, and yet his block met resistance—I could see his forearm compress against something, the muscles engage, the trajectory redirect—and when I asked what he was blocking, he said, "Thursday's class." I wrote this down and asked him to repeat it. He said it again. He was blocking a strike that a classmate would throw in three days. The block would be ready when the strike arrived. I asked if this didn't present a causality problem. He looked at me the way Dahl had looked at me. Patient. Linguistic. As if "causality" were a dialect he'd heard of but didn't use in daily speech.

Station 4555, an unregistered dojo operating out of a storage rental, which I should have flagged for immediate decertification but did not, because I was beginning to suspect that the concept of certification was what you might call *under review.* Bridge Sequence, movement 14: the rooted pivot. The standard specifies that the practitioner's left foot remains planted while the torso rotates one hundred eighty degrees. In this space, a teenage girl with braids and a gi that was two sizes too big performed the rooted pivot. Her left foot remained planted. Her torso rotated one hundred eighty degrees. Then her torso kept rotating. Two-seventy. Three-sixty. Her foot had not moved. Her foot was on the mat. I confirmed this visually. Her foot was on the mat and it was also not on the mat. Gunpowder Rendezvous

Spike Spiegel & Revy

Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff.

**Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)**
Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew.
Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens."

**Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)**
Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation.
